planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix; this variegated form is particularly susceptible to root rot, so never allow the pot to sit in standing water. Maintain warm temperatures above 60°F and high humidity.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix, allowing the top inch or two to dry before watering again. This variegated form of the classic zebra alocasia carries the same striking dark brown-and-cream banded, snakeskin-patterned petioles as the plain species, but the arrow-shaped leaf blades themselves are irregularly splashed and marbled in white, giving the whole plant a two-tiered ornamental effect between stem and leaf. Because the pale leaf tissue photosynthesizes less efficiently, this cultivar grows more slowly and needs slightly brighter light than the plain green-leaved species to stay vigorous and avoid reverting. Keep it warm and humid, out of direct sun, which can scorch the leaf surface, and stake tall petioles if they begin to lean under the weight of larger leaves.

planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix; Nebula is particularly susceptible to root rot, so never allow the pot to sit in standing water. Maintain warm temperatures above 60°F and high humidity.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix, allowing the top inch or two to dry before watering again. Nebula is a hybrid alocasia with thick, dusty grey-green leaves overlaid by soft, cloud-like patches and darker venation that seem to drift across the leaf surface, giving it a hazy, atmospheric look distinct from the sharply defined patterns of alocasias like Amazonica or Polly. Its compact size and slow growth make it well suited to a bright windowsill or grow-light shelf rather than a large floor plant. Keep it warm and humid, out of direct sun, which can scorch the leaf surface, and repot only when clearly rootbound, since alocasias generally prefer being slightly snug in their pots.

planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix; Bisma is particularly susceptible to root rot, so never allow the pot to sit in standing water. Maintain warm temperatures above 60°F and high humidity.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix, allowing the top inch or two to dry before watering again. Bisma is a slow-growing hybrid alocasia in the same textured-leaf group as Alocasia melo and Maharani, with thick, stiff, grey-green leaves showing a rough, slightly pebbled surface and prominent sunken venation, giving it a sturdy, sculptural presence distinct from the glossy, thin-textured foliage of most other alocasias. Its compact size and slow habit make it a good choice for collectors with limited bright-light space. Keep it warm and humid, out of direct sun, which can scorch the leaf surface, and avoid overwatering, since thick-leaved alocasias in this group are especially prone to root and stem rot in soggy mix.

planting.note: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix; Low Rider is particularly susceptible to root rot, so never allow the pot to sit in standing water. Maintain warm temperatures above 60°F and high humidity.

directions: Grow in bright indirect light in very well-drained, chunky, perlite-enriched aroid mix, allowing the top inch or two to dry before watering again. Low Rider is a dwarf hybrid alocasia with dark, thick, arrow-shaped leaves held very close to the soil on unusually short petioles, giving the whole plant a squat, ground-hugging silhouette quite different from the tall, upright habit of most alocasias. Its small footprint and slow growth make it especially well suited to a crowded plant shelf or terrarium-style display where taller alocasias would quickly outgrow the space. Keep it warm and humid, out of direct sun, which can scorch the leaf surface, and avoid overwatering, since compact alocasia hybrids are often more prone to rot than their larger relatives.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Compactstar is an excellent tropical shade perennial for zone 9b-11 gardens or as a smaller-scale container plant brought indoors in winter in cooler zones.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic soil in partial to full shade; Compactstar is intolerant of drought, direct sun, and cold temperatures below 50°F. This dwarf selection of the popular never-never plant carries the same silver and dark green striped, feathery-patterned foliage as the species, but on a noticeably smaller, denser, more compact clump, making it a better fit for smaller containers, tabletops, and tighter garden spaces than the larger standard form. Like its parent, the paddle-shaped leaves fold upward at night in a mild nyctinastic movement and relax flat during the day. Keep soil evenly moist, provide bright indirect light to partial shade, and divide congested clumps in spring to propagate or refresh the planting.

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors. Triostar is one of the more demanding stromanthes, needing consistently high humidity and filtered or rain water.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light — no direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil. Triostar is one of the most popular variegated tropical foliage plants, with long, glossy, dark green leaves irregularly splashed and streaked in cream and white, backed by a vivid magenta-pink underside that shows dramatically whenever the leaves fold or catch a breeze. Like its close relatives the calatheas and marantas, it performs a nyctinastic leaf movement, folding upright at night to reveal the hot-pink reverse and relaxing flat during the day. It is more demanding than many tropical foliage plants, wanting consistently high humidity, evenly moist but never soggy soil, and filtered or rain water rather than tap water, since brown, crispy leaf edges quickly follow low humidity or mineral sensitivity. In zone 9 it thrives as a shaded porch container plant in summer but must move indoors well before temperatures drop into the 50s.

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors. Stripestar needs consistently high humidity and filtered or rain water.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light — no direct sun — in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil. Stripestar is a close relative of the better-known Triostar, carrying the same vivid magenta-pink leaf underside, but with finer, more numerous, closely spaced white pinstripes running the length of each dark green leaf rather than Triostar's broader, more irregular cream splashes, giving it a crisper, more linear variegation pattern. Like other stromanthes it performs a nyctinastic leaf movement, folding upright at night to flash the pink reverse and relaxing flat during the day. It wants consistently high humidity, evenly moist but never soggy soil, and filtered or rain water to avoid brown leaf-edge scorch. In zone 9 it grows well as a shaded porch container plant through the warm season, moving indoors before temperatures fall into the 50s.

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, peat-based, slightly acidic (pH 5.5-6.5) soil in bright indirect shade; maranta requires consistent moisture, high humidity, and warmth above 60°F. Avoid hard water — use rainwater or allow tap water to sit 24 hours before using.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, peat-based soil in bright indirect shade. Rabbit's Foot is the classic and most widely grown prayer plant form, with oval, pale to medium green leaves marked by rows of dark olive-brown to purplish-green blotches flanking the central vein, a pattern often likened to a row of paw prints or feet marching down the leaf, which gives the variety its common name. Like other marantas it performs a striking daily leaf movement, lying flat to catch light during the day and folding upright like praying hands at night, an easy visual cue that the plant is happy and well watered. Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged, provide high humidity where possible, and divide congested clumps in spring to propagate or refresh an aging plant.

common_name: Red Vein Prayer Plant (Erythroneura Maranta, Herringbone Plant)

planting.note: Plant divisions in moist, peat-based, slightly acidic (pH 5.5-6.5) soil in bright indirect shade; maranta requires consistent moisture, high humidity, and warmth above 60°F. Avoid hard water — use rainwater or allow tap water to sit 24 hours before using.

directions: Plant in moist, slightly acidic, peat-based soil in bright indirect shade. Red Vein is the most vividly colored prayer plant variety, with dark olive-green leaves marked by bright red-pink veins radiating out from the midrib and paler green blotches along the veins, giving it a bolder, more jewel-toned look than the plainer Rabbit's Foot variety, with a deep maroon-red leaf underside that shows whenever the leaves fold. Like other marantas it performs a daily leaf movement, lying flat during the day and folding upright at night, and appreciates slightly brighter light than other maranta varieties to bring out the strongest vein color, though still no direct sun. Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged, provide high humidity, and divide congested clumps in spring to propagate.

common_name: White Star Calathea (Pink-White Striped Prayer Plant)

planting.note: Move outdoors to a shaded location after temperatures remain reliably above 55°F; in zone 9 place outdoors April-October and overwinter indoors.

directions: Plant in deep shade to bright indirect light in well-drained, humus-rich, consistently moist, slightly acidic soil. White Star carries long, lance-shaped leaves striped in alternating bands of pink, cream, and dark green radiating out from the midrib, a bold pastel pattern related to the popular pink-striped calathea and stromanthe cultivars but with a distinct, more star-like symmetry to the striping. As with other prayer plants, leaves fold upright at night and relax flat during the day. Maintain consistently moist soil and high humidity, and use filtered or rain water when possible, since brown leaf edges are usually a sign of low humidity or tap-water mineral sensitivity. In zone 9 it grows well as a shaded porch or patio container plant through the warm season, moving indoors before temperatures fall into the 50s.
